prompt: Which statement best defines water quality in aquaculture?

options.text: The adjustment of mineral salts solely to eliminate all indigenous algae.
The suitability of the physical, chemical and biological characteristics of water for fish survival, growth and health.
The density of hydrogen particles required to prevent every form of microbial life.
The complete removal of every organic substance from water by crystallisation.

explanation: Test 2, question 6, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. Three parameter families, one purpose: physical, chemical and biological characteristics, judged by whether fish survive, grow and stay healthy.

why.a: Wrong. Solely and all are absolutes, and plankton is beneficial in moderation rather than something to eliminate.
why.b: Correct. Physical, chemical and biological, measured against fish survival, growth and health.
why.c: Wrong. Every form is an absolute, and beneficial bacteria such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are wanted in the water.
why.d: Wrong. Complete and every are absolutes, and organic matter is a natural part of the ecosystem.

prompt: Water quality in fish farming refers to the optimal physical, chemical and {{1}} parameters of water.
explanation: Biological. The three families are physical, chemical and biological, and biological is the one candidates leave out.

prompt: In simple terms, water quality is the {{1}} of water that will make the fishes thrive or live a happy life.
explanation: Standard. The examiner reused the same word in Test 1, where the thumb rule is not to venture in without knowing the standard of your water.

prompt: How does the text describe the entire aquatic environment?

options.text: An ecosystem comprising the fish and other living organisms, plants and animals
A sterile container holding only fish and water
A closed chemical system with no living component
A storage tank whose contents do not interact

explanation: An ecosystem. That is why biological parameters exist at all: the fish share the water with plankton, bacteria, plants and parasites.

why.a: Correct. The text calls it an ecosystem of fish, other living organisms, plants and animals.
why.b: Wrong. A sterile tank would have no beneficial bacteria and no natural feed.
why.c: Wrong. The living component is the whole point of the biological parameters.
why.d: Wrong. The interactions are exactly what water quality management manages.

prompt: Maintaining optimal water conditions is crucial for which three outcomes?

options.text: Preventing diseases, ensuring efficient growth, and maximising yields
Reducing feed costs, raising prices, and shortening transport
Meeting export quotas, avoiding tax, and securing loans
Attracting tourists, training staff, and keeping records

explanation: Disease prevention, efficient growth, maximum yield. Those three are what good water buys you.

why.a: Correct. These three are named in the water quality section.
why.b: Wrong. Feed cost is addressed by feed production, not by water quality directly.
why.c: Wrong. None of these appears in the water quality section.
why.d: Wrong. These belong to tourism, training and the MANAGE phase.

prompt: What does the text say poor water quality leads to?

options.text: Stress, disease outbreaks, slow growth, and high mortality rates
Faster growth but smaller fish
Reduced feed consumption with no other effect
Improved colour and marketability

explanation: Four consequences, and they compound: stress leads to disease, disease slows growth, and severe cases kill.

why.a: Correct. These four are listed together in the text.
why.b: Wrong. Poor water slows growth; it does not accelerate it.
why.c: Wrong. Reduced feeding is one symptom among several, not the whole effect.
why.d: Wrong. Poor water produces poor skin and fin condition, making fish less marketable.

prompt: Good water quality ensures healthy fish, high productivity and {{1}}.
explanation: Profitability. The text always closes the water quality argument on the money, which is why it calls water quality a core area to master.

prompt: Water quality is central to which of the following?

options.text: A successful fish-farming business.
Automating every feeding operation without human supervision.
Reducing the shipping weight of commercial feed.
Determining national agricultural tax exemptions.

explanation: Test 2, question 1, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. The text calls water quality a core area to master for a successful fish farming business, and returns to it as the thumb rule.

why.a: Correct. Water quality is core to a successful fish farming business.
why.b: Wrong. Automated feeders are a MULTIPLY technology, and every without supervision is an absolute.
why.c: Wrong. Shipping weight of feed is not discussed anywhere in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Tax exemptions appear nowhere in the course.

prompt: Water quality management is one of the core areas to master for a successful fish farming business.
explanation: Stated directly, and reinforced by the thumb rule that closes the section: do not venture into fish farming without knowing the quality of your water.

why.true: Correct. The text names water quality management as a core area to master.
why.false: Wrong. The whole section exists to make the opposite case.

prompt: Which of the following is considered a "Physical Parameter" of water quality?

options.text: Turbidity, odor, and temperature
Ammonia, salinity, and pH
Nitrite, Nitrate, and Iron
Bacteria, viruses, and algae

explanation: Test 1, question 2, quoted as printed. The three families sort cleanly: physical is what you can see, feel or smell; chemical is what is dissolved; biological is what is alive.

why.a: Correct. Turbidity, odour and temperature are all physical parameters.
why.b: Wrong. Ammonia, salinity and pH are chemical parameters.
why.c: Wrong. Nitrite, nitrate and iron are chemical parameters.
why.d: Wrong. Bacteria, viruses and algae are biological parameters.

prompt: A fish farmer observes high water temperature and cloudy water caused by suspended particles. Under which classification do these indicators fall?

options.text: Chemical parameters, which include iron, ammonia, salinity, pH and hardness.
Mechanical parameters, which include filter replacement, aeration rate and tank thickness.
Biological parameters, which include fungi, bacteria, viruses, parasites and algae.
Physical parameters, which include turbidity, colour, odour, temperature and suspended solids.

explanation: Test 2, question 26, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. Temperature and cloudiness from suspended particles are the two clearest physical parameters, temperature and turbidity.

why.a: Wrong. Those five are the chemical parameters.
why.b: Wrong. There is no mechanical parameter family in the course; it is invented.
why.c: Wrong. Those five are the biological parameters.
why.d: Correct. Turbidity, colour, odour, temperature and suspended solids are the physical parameters.

prompt: Temperature is the degree of hotness or {{1}} of the water.
explanation: Coldness. Temperature affects fish metabolism, feeding, breeding and growth rates, which is why it heads the physical parameters.

prompt: Which four processes does the text say temperature affects?

options.text: Fish metabolism, feeding, breeding and growth rates
Pond depth, bank strength, fencing and lighting
Market price, transport cost, packaging and branding
Only breeding, since the others are unaffected

explanation: Metabolism, feeding, breeding, growth. Temperature reaches all four, which is why a heater or chiller appears in the stress remedies.

why.a: Correct. These four are the key facts about temperature.
why.b: Wrong. Those are construction matters, from the MAKE principles.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to marketing.
why.d: Wrong, and the word only contradicts the list of four.

prompt: Why does warmer water hold less oxygen?

options.text: As temperature increases, the solubility of oxygen in water decreases
Warm water evaporates the oxygen into the air as a gas of its own
Warm water blocks photosynthesis completely at all depths
Warm water converts oxygen directly into ammonia

explanation: Solubility falls as temperature rises. The consequence the text draws is stark: even if oxygen is being produced by photosynthesis, the water cannot hold as much of it.

why.a: Correct. Rising temperature reduces the solubility of oxygen in water.
why.b: Wrong. The text explains it by solubility, not by evaporation.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. It is turbidity that blocks sunlight, and not completely.
why.d: Wrong. Ammonia comes from fish waste and uneaten feed, not from oxygen.

prompt: As water temperature rises, the amount of oxygen the water can hold also rises.
explanation: The reverse. Warmer water holds less oxygen because solubility falls as temperature increases, which is why heat and low oxygen so often arrive together.

why.true: Wrong. This inverts the relationship the text states.
why.false: Correct. Warmer water holds less oxygen, not more.

prompt: At what temperature does the text say tilapia thrives?

options.text: 25 to 30 degrees Celsius
5 to 8 degrees Celsius
6.5 to 8.5 degrees Celsius
40 degrees Celsius

explanation: 25 to 30 degrees Celsius. Note the traps: 5 to 8 is the dissolved oxygen range in mg/L, 6.5 to 8.5 is the pH range, and 40 degrees is the oil palm dormancy treatment.

why.a: Correct. Tilapia thrives at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius.
why.b: Wrong. 5 to 8 mg/L is the dissolved oxygen requirement, not a temperature.
why.c: Wrong. 6.5 to 8.5 is the pH range, which has no units of temperature.
why.d: Wrong. 40 degrees for 70 to 80 days breaks oil palm seed dormancy in Module Three.

prompt: Optimal temperature varies by species, and tilapia thrives at 25 to {{1}} degrees Celsius.
explanation: 30. Keep it apart from the oil palm optimum of 25 to 34 degrees, which shares its lower bound.

prompt: What is turbidity, and what does excess turbidity do?

options.text: It is water clarity, and excess turbidity from suspended particles or algae blocks sunlight and reduces oxygen production
It is water hardness, and excess turbidity raises the pH
It is water temperature, and excess turbidity cools the pond
It is the count of bacteria, and excess turbidity indicates disease

explanation: Clarity. The mechanism matters: blocked sunlight means less photosynthesis, and less photosynthesis means less oxygen.

why.a: Correct. Turbidity is water clarity, and excess blocks sunlight and reduces oxygen production.
why.b: Wrong. Hardness is a chemical parameter, separate from turbidity.
why.c: Wrong. Temperature is its own physical parameter.
why.d: Wrong. Bacterial counts are a biological parameter.

prompt: Why does dissolved oxygen fall at night in a pond with heavy phytoplankton?

options.text: There is no photosynthesis, and both the phytoplankton and the fish respire, consuming oxygen
The water cools, which destroys the dissolved oxygen
The fish stop breathing at night, so oxygen readings become inaccurate
Ammonia converts the oxygen into nitrite after dark

explanation: Photosynthesis stops but respiration does not. Both the algae and the fish are drawing oxygen from the same water, which is why night is when fish come gasping to the surface.

why.a: Correct. No photosynthesis at night, and both phytoplankton and fish respire.
why.b: Wrong. Cooler water actually holds more oxygen, not less.
why.c: Wrong. Fish respire continuously, which is part of the problem.
why.d: Wrong. Nitrite comes from the breakdown of waste, not from oxygen.

prompt: During the day dissolved oxygen increases because of {{1}}, which benefits the fish.
explanation: Photosynthesis. The daily swing between photosynthesis and respiration is what makes plankton both useful and dangerous.

prompt: What is the condition called when the oxygen level in the water is low?

options.text: Hypoxia
Eutrophication
Turbidity
Salinity

explanation: Hypoxia, defined in the glossary as a deficiency of oxygen in a specific environment such as water, air or living tissues. Its signs in fish are stress, surface gasping and, in severe cases, death.

why.a: Correct. Low oxygen is hypoxia.
why.b: Wrong. Eutrophication is over-enrichment with nutrients, which can cause hypoxia but is not the same thing.
why.c: Wrong. Turbidity is water clarity.
why.d: Wrong. Salinity is a chemical parameter, the salt content.

prompt: If the oxygen level is low, a condition called {{1}}, the fish may become stressed, come to the surface gasping for air, or even die.
explanation: Hypoxia. Surface gasping is the sign that appears in three of the four behaviour categories, and low oxygen is behind all of them.

prompt: What two long-term effects does the text give for excess phytoplankton in a pond?

options.text: Eutrophication, and toxin production by species such as blue-green algae
Increased water hardness, and rising salinity
Iron precipitation, and filter clogging
Reduced turbidity, and clearer water

explanation: Eutrophication and toxin production. Blue-green algae, the cyanobacteria, are the species named as producing toxic materials harmful to fish and other aquatic life.

why.a: Correct. Both are named as long-term effects of excess phytoplankton.
why.b: Wrong. Hardness and salinity are chemical parameters unconnected to this effect.
why.c: Wrong. Those are iron problems, from a different part of the section.
why.d: Wrong. Excess phytoplankton increases turbidity rather than reducing it.

prompt: Some phytoplankton species, like {{1}} algae, produce toxic materials harmful to fish and other aquatic life.
explanation: Blue-green algae, also named as cyanobacteria in the biological parameters. They are the toxin producers.

prompt: During a water-quality assessment, a technician measures ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals. Under which group do these measurements fall?

options.text: Physical parameters.
Chemical parameters.
Operational parameters.
Biological parameters.

explanation: Test 2, question 5, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. Anything dissolved and measured by concentration is chemical.

why.a: Wrong. Physical parameters are temperature, turbidity, colour, odour and suspended solids.
why.b: Correct. Ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals are all chemical.
why.c: Wrong. There is no operational parameter family in the course; it is invented.
why.d: Wrong. Biological parameters are the living organisms in the water.

prompt: Ammonia, salinity, pH, {{1}} and dissolved minerals are all chemical parameters of water.
explanation: Hardness. It is the item in the chemical list that appears nowhere else in the course, so it is easy to forget.

prompt: The stated pH range suitable for rearing fish is 6.5 to {{1}} .
explanation: Test 2, question 22, quoted as printed. 6.5 to 8.5. Do not confuse it with dissolved oxygen at 5 to 8 mg/L, which is the trap Test 1 set in question 1.

prompt: What is the ideal pH range for most fish?

options.text: 5 to 8

explanation: 6.5 to 8.5. The three wrong options are all real figures from elsewhere in the course, which is exactly how the examiner builds a numeric question.

why.a: Correct. The ideal pH range for most fish is 6.5 to 8.5.
why.b: Wrong. 5 to 8 mg/L is the dissolved oxygen requirement.
why.c: Wrong. 5.0 to 6.0 is the soil pH for oil palm, from Module Three.
why.d: Wrong. 0.1 to 0.5 mg/L is the moderate risk band for iron.

prompt: What does the text say extreme pH levels cause, and how is pH corrected?

options.text: They cause stress, poor growth and even death, and pH is corrected by adding synthetic inorganic chemicals
They cause faster growth, and pH is corrected by adding more feed
They have no measurable effect, so no correction is needed
They cause only colour change, corrected by increasing aeration

explanation: Stress, poor growth, death, and correction by synthetic inorganic chemicals. Aeration is the answer for oxygen and carbon dioxide, not for pH.

why.a: Correct. Both halves come straight from the pH entry.
why.b: Wrong. Extreme pH harms growth rather than helping it.
why.c: Wrong. The text names three serious effects.
why.d: Wrong. Colour is a physical parameter, and aeration addresses oxygen and carbon dioxide.

prompt: In terms of physico-chemical parameters, which of the following represents the "Ideal Range" for Dissolved Oxygen (DO) to ensure healthy fish growth?

options.text: 5 – 8 mg/L

explanation: Test 1, question 1, quoted as printed. The dissolved oxygen minimum is 5 to 8 mg/L. The 6.5 to 8.5 answer is the pH range wearing an mg/L unit, which is the trap.

why.a: Wrong. 25 to 30 degrees Celsius is the tilapia temperature range, not an oxygen concentration.
why.b: Wrong. Below 0.05 mg/L is the ammonia toxicity threshold.
why.c: Wrong. 6.5 to 8.5 is the pH range, and pH has no units; the mg/L here is bait.
why.d: Correct. The minimum dissolved oxygen requirement is 5 to 8 mg/L, varying by species.

prompt: The minimum dissolved oxygen requirement is {{1}} mg/L, varying by species.
explanation: 5 to 8 mg/L. Say it aloud with its unit every time, because pH at 6.5 to 8.5 is deliberately close and carries no unit at all.

prompt: How is dissolved oxygen managed on a fish farm?

options.text: By water exchange and aeration
By adding synthetic inorganic chemicals
By raising the water temperature
By increasing stocking density

explanation: Water exchange and aeration. The same pair manages carbon dioxide, and aeration alone is the remedy for slow movement in the behaviour unit.

why.a: Correct. Low dissolved oxygen is managed by water exchange and aeration.
why.b: Wrong. Synthetic inorganic chemicals correct pH.
why.c: Wrong. Raising the temperature lowers the oxygen the water can hold.
why.d: Wrong. Higher stocking density means more respiration and less oxygen.

prompt: Above what level does the text say ammonia becomes toxic and can cause gill damage?

options.text: 0.1 mg/L
20 mg/L
50 mg/L

explanation: Above 0.05 mg/L. The four chemical thresholds are worth learning as a set: ammonia above 0.05, nitrite below 0.1, nitrate above 50, carbon dioxide above 20.

why.a: Correct. High ammonia above 0.05 mg/L is toxic and damages gills.
why.b: Wrong. 0.1 mg/L is the ceiling for nitrite.
why.c: Wrong. 20 mg/L is the carbon dioxide level that suffocates fish.
why.d: Wrong. 50 mg/L is the nitrate level that affects fish health.

prompt: Ammonia and nitrite are produced from fish waste and {{1}} feed.
explanation: Uneaten feed. This is the chemistry behind the rule against overfeeding, and behind the Test 2 answer that overfeeding leads to water pollution.

prompt: Nitrite levels should remain below which figure to prevent poisoning?

options.text: 0.1 mg/L
5 mg/L
50 mg/L

explanation: Below 0.1 mg/L. Ammonia and nitrite are the pair produced by waste and uneaten feed, and their thresholds, 0.05 and 0.1, are close enough to be worth drilling apart.

why.a: Correct. Nitrite should stay below 0.1 mg/L.
why.b: Wrong. 0.05 mg/L is the ammonia toxicity threshold.
why.c: Wrong. 5 mg/L is the bottom of the dissolved oxygen range.
why.d: Wrong. 50 mg/L is the nitrate figure.

prompt: Nitrate is less toxic than nitrite, but high levels above {{1}} mg/L can affect fish health.
explanation: 50 mg/L. Nitrate is controlled through water exchange and plant filtration in integrated systems, which is where aquaponics earns its keep.

prompt: How is nitrate controlled, according to the text?

options.text: Through water exchange and plant filtration in integrated systems
By adding lime or potassium permanganate
By raising the stocking density
By increasing the feeding rate

explanation: Water exchange and plant filtration. Plant filtration is the aquaponic principle: the crops take up the nutrients the fish produce.

why.a: Correct. Both methods are named in the nitrate entry.
why.b: Wrong. Lime and potassium permanganate are iron treatments.
why.c: Wrong. Higher density means more waste and more nitrate.
why.d: Wrong. More feed means more waste, which raises nitrate.

prompt: Above what level does the text say carbon dioxide can suffocate fish by interfering with oxygen uptake?

options.text: 20 mg/L
0.1 mg/L
8.5 mg/L
50 mg/L

explanation: Above 20 mg/L. Like dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide is managed through aeration and water exchange.

why.a: Correct. High carbon dioxide above 20 mg/L suffocates fish.
why.b: Wrong. 0.1 mg/L is the nitrite ceiling.
why.c: Wrong. 8.5 is the top of the pH range and carries no unit.
why.d: Wrong. 50 mg/L is the nitrate figure.

prompt: High carbon dioxide levels are managed through {{1}} and water exchange.
explanation: Aeration. It is the single most useful intervention in the course: it raises oxygen, drives off carbon dioxide, and oxidises iron.

prompt: How can the presence of iron in water be spotted without a test kit?

options.text: Silvery films on the surface, and brownish sediment at the bottom of water left standing in a bucket
A sweet smell and a green tint
Foam on the surface after rainfall
Fish gathering at the feeding point

explanation: Silvery films and brownish sediment. The full picture also includes reddish-brown staining that discolours the water.

why.a: Correct. Both signs are given in the iron entry.
why.b: Wrong. Odour and colour are physical parameters, but these are not the iron signs.
why.c: Wrong. Foam is not mentioned anywhere in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Gathering at the feeding point is a hunger behaviour.

prompt: Which set gives the acceptable iron levels for fish farming?

options.text: Safe below 0.1 mg/L, moderate risk 0.1 to 0.5 mg/L, high risk above 0.5 mg/L
Safe below 5 mg/L, moderate risk 5 to 8 mg/L, high risk above 8 mg/L
Safe below 20 mg/L, moderate risk 20 to 50 mg/L, high risk above 50 mg/L
Safe below 6.5, moderate risk 6.5 to 8.5, high risk above 8.5

explanation: Three bands: below 0.1 ideal, 0.1 to 0.5 moderate, above 0.5 high risk. Excessive iron above 0.5 mg/L is toxic, causing stress, reduced growth and gill damage.

why.a: Correct. These are the three iron bands the text gives.
why.b: Wrong. 5 to 8 mg/L is the dissolved oxygen range.
why.c: Wrong. 20 and 50 mg/L are the carbon dioxide and nitrate figures.
why.d: Wrong. 6.5 to 8.5 is the pH range.

prompt: For iron in fish farming water, the moderate risk band runs from 0.1 to {{1}} mg/L.
explanation: 0.5 mg/L, which is also where high risk begins. Below 0.1 is the ideal safe limit.

prompt: Excessive iron above 0.5 mg/L is toxic to fish. What does the text say it causes?

options.text: Stress, reduced growth and gill damage, with iron deposits on gills reducing oxygen absorption and leading to hypoxia
Rapid growth followed by early maturity
Improved colour and higher market value
A rise in dissolved oxygen levels

explanation: The chain is physical: iron settles on the gills, the gills absorb less oxygen, and the fish becomes hypoxic even in oxygenated water.

why.a: Correct. Stress, reduced growth, gill damage, and hypoxia from deposits on the gills.
why.b: Wrong. Iron toxicity slows growth.
why.c: Wrong. Iron discolours the water and harms the fish.
why.d: Wrong. Iron reduces the oxygen the fish can take up.

prompt: Iron deposits on {{1}} reduce oxygen absorption, leading to hypoxia.
explanation: Gills. High ammonia damages gills too, so gill damage is the shared symptom of two different chemical problems.

prompt: Which iron bacteria does the text name as forming slimy biofilms that clog gills?

options.text: Gallionella and Leptothrix
Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter
Aeromonas and Pseudomonas
Saprolegnia and Gyrodactylus

explanation: Gallionella and Leptothrix. Keep the four bacterial pairs of this course apart: iron bacteria, beneficial nitrifiers, harmful pathogens, and the fungus and parasite pair.

why.a: Correct. Gallionella and Leptothrix are the iron bacteria named.
why.b: Wrong. Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are the beneficial bacteria that break down ammonia and nitrate.
why.c: Wrong. Aeromonas and Pseudomonas are harmful bacteria causing infections.
why.d: Wrong. Saprolegnia is a fungus and Gyrodactylus a parasite.

prompt: High iron levels promote iron bacteria such as Gallionella and {{1}}, which form slimy biofilms.
explanation: Leptothrix. The biofilms clog gills and reduce oxygen availability, which is the same end result as the iron deposits themselves.

prompt: What visible effect does high iron have on the water itself?

options.text: Reddish-brown staining that reduces transparency and light penetration
A permanent blue tint that improves clarity
Total loss of odour
A rise in water temperature

explanation: Reddish-brown discolouration, which reduces light penetration and hinders aquatic plant and algae growth. Less light means less photosynthesis, and less photosynthesis means less oxygen.

why.a: Correct. The text names reddish-brown stains and reduced transparency.
why.b: Wrong. Iron stains reddish-brown, and it worsens clarity.
why.c: Wrong. Odour is a physical parameter; iron is not said to remove it.
why.d: Wrong. Iron does not change temperature.

prompt: Which four symptoms does the text give for long-term iron exposure in fish?

options.text: Lethargy, loss of appetite, difficulty breathing and abnormal swimming
Rapid growth, bright colour, high appetite and active swimming
Clamped fins, faded colour, hiding and erratic swimming
Begging at the surface, lunging at food and gathering at the feeding spot

explanation: Lethargy, appetite loss, breathing difficulty, abnormal swimming. Note how close the clamped fins and faded colour answer is: those are the stress signs, and the overlap is deliberate.

why.a: Correct. These four are the iron toxicity symptoms.
why.b: Wrong. These are signs of healthy fish.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the stress behaviour signs from the behaviour unit.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the hunger behaviour signs.

prompt: In recirculating aquaculture systems and aerated ponds, what does iron do to the equipment?

options.text: It oxidises and precipitates into rust-like deposits that clog filters, pipes and aeration systems
It lubricates pumps and extends their service life
It has no effect on equipment at any concentration
It dissolves plastic pipework

explanation: Rust-like deposits that clog filters, pipes and aeration systems, reducing efficiency and raising maintenance costs.

why.a: Correct. Oxidation and precipitation into rust-like deposits is what the text describes.
why.b: Wrong. Iron raises maintenance costs rather than lowering them.
why.c: Wrong. The text devotes a whole heading to filter clogging and system damage.
why.d: Wrong. No dissolving of pipework is claimed.

prompt: Iron oxidation can alter water chemistry, making {{1}} unstable, which further stresses fish.
explanation: pH. Iron therefore attacks on four fronts: the fish directly, the water quality, the equipment and the pH stability.

prompt: How does aeration and oxidation remove iron from water?

options.text: It converts soluble iron, Fe2+, into insoluble iron, Fe3+, which can then be filtered out
It evaporates the iron as a gas
It dissolves the iron so it passes harmlessly through the fish
It binds the iron to ammonia, which is then removed

explanation: Soluble to insoluble. Once the iron is insoluble it can be trapped by sand filters, activated carbon or iron-removal filters.

why.a: Correct. Exposure to air converts Fe2+ to Fe3+, which is filterable.
why.b: Wrong. Iron does not leave as a gas.
why.c: Wrong. The point is to make it less soluble, not more.
why.d: Wrong. Ammonia is a separate problem, broken down by beneficial bacteria.

prompt: Aeration converts soluble iron into {{1}} iron, which can be filtered out.
explanation: Insoluble. Fe2+ becomes Fe3+, and only then can a filter catch it.

prompt: Which chemicals does the text name for treating excess iron?

options.text: Lime or potassium permanganate
Chlorine or bleach
Formalin or malachite green
Salt or sugar

explanation: Lime or potassium permanganate. The other iron measures are aeration, filtration, water source selection and regular testing.

why.a: Correct. These two are the chemical treatments named for iron.
why.b: Wrong. Chlorine appears only as something to remove from tap water when conditioning an aquarium.
why.c: Wrong. Neither is mentioned in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Salinity is a parameter, but salt is not given as an iron treatment.

prompt: What are biological parameters?

options.text: The living organisms present in water that can affect fish health, growth and overall farm productivity
The dissolved gases in the water
The temperature and clarity of the water
The mineral content of the pond bed

explanation: Living organisms. Maintaining a balanced biological environment is described as crucial for disease prevention, water quality management and sustainable fish farming.

why.a: Correct. Biological parameters are the living organisms in the water.
why.b: Wrong. Dissolved gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide are chemical.
why.c: Wrong. Temperature and clarity are physical.
why.d: Wrong. Minerals dissolved in the water are chemical.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five key biological parameters in fish farming?

options.text: Plankton
Microbial load
Turbidity
Macrophytes

explanation: The five are plankton, microbial load, pathogens and parasites, organic matter and decomposers, and macrophytes. Turbidity is physical.

why.a: Wrong as an answer. Plankton is the first biological parameter.
why.b: Wrong as an answer. Microbial load covers bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa.
why.c: Correct. Turbidity is a physical parameter, water clarity.
why.d: Wrong as an answer. Macrophytes are aquatic plants and weeds.

prompt: The text lists {{1}} key biological parameters in fish farming.
explanation: Five: plankton, microbial load, pathogens and parasites, organic matter and decomposers, and macrophytes.

prompt: What role does plankton play, and what is its risk?

options.text: It is essential for natural fish feed and oxygen production, but excessive growth causes eutrophication, reducing oxygen and stressing fish
It has no useful role and should be eliminated entirely
It only matters in marine systems, not in ponds
It raises the pH beyond the safe range

explanation: Useful in moderation, dangerous in excess. Moderate plankton blooms improve water quality; excessive growth is eutrophication.

why.a: Correct. Natural feed and oxygen production, against eutrophication in excess.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Plankton is essential natural feed.
why.c: Wrong. The text discusses plankton in ponds throughout.
why.d: Wrong. Plankton's stated risks are oxygen depletion and toxins, not pH.

prompt: Plankton covers both phytoplankton and {{1}}.
explanation: Zooplankton. Phytoplankton photosynthesises and so drives the day and night oxygen swing; zooplankton is animal plankton.

prompt: What three things can algal blooms such as cyanobacteria do?

options.text: Produce toxins, reduce oxygen at night, and cause fish kills
Raise the water temperature, lower the pH, and clear the water
Increase dissolved oxygen at night and improve growth
Remove ammonia and nitrite entirely from the system

explanation: Toxins, night-time oxygen depletion, fish kills. Cyanobacteria are the blue-green algae named in the turbidity discussion.

why.a: Correct. These three risks are named under plankton.
why.b: Wrong. Blooms increase turbidity rather than clearing water.
why.c: Wrong. At night blooms consume oxygen; they do not produce it.
why.d: Wrong. Ammonia and nitrate breakdown is the work of Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter.

prompt: Which bacteria does the text name as beneficial, helping in ammonia and nitrate breakdown?

options.text: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter
Aeromonas and Vibrio
Gallionella and Leptothrix
Ichthyophthirius and Gyrodactylus

explanation: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter. Preserving them is exactly why filter media are rinsed in tank water rather than tap water during monthly maintenance.

why.a: Correct. These are the beneficial bacteria named.
why.b: Wrong. Aeromonas and Vibrio are harmful bacteria that cause infections.
why.c: Wrong. Gallionella and Leptothrix are iron bacteria that clog gills.
why.d: Wrong. Those are parasites that weaken fish.

prompt: The beneficial bacteria Nitrosomonas and {{1}} help in ammonia and nitrate breakdown.
explanation: Nitrobacter. The two nitrifiers share a prefix, which makes them easy to hold together and hard to confuse with the harmful trio.

prompt: Poor sanitation, overfeeding and the accumulation of organic waste in a pond can lead to which problem?

options.text: Automatic restoration of all water-quality parameters without water management.
Excessive bacterial growth, including harmful strains such as Aeromonas and Pseudomonas.
Rapid deterioration of glass solely because of the microbial plate count.
The complete conversion of toxic ammonia into harmless gases without treatment.

explanation: Test 2, question 24, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. The harmful bacteria named in the text are Aeromonas, Vibrio and Pseudomonas.

why.a: Wrong. Automatic and all are absolutes, and water quality does not restore itself.
why.b: Correct. Excess organic waste drives bacterial growth, including Aeromonas and Pseudomonas.
why.c: Wrong. Solely is an absolute, and glass deterioration is not a claim the course makes.
why.d: Wrong. Complete and without treatment are absolutes; ammonia breakdown depends on beneficial bacteria.

prompt: The harmful bacteria that cause infections are Aeromonas, {{1}} and Pseudomonas.
explanation: Vibrio. Test 2 quoted only two of the three, Aeromonas and Pseudomonas, so Vibrio is the one most likely to be missed.

prompt: Which viruses and which fungus does the text name in the microbial load?

options.text: Iridovirus and koi herpesvirus, and the fungus Saprolegnia
Rotavirus and influenza, and the fungus Candida
Iridovirus and rabies, and the fungus Aspergillus
Koi herpesvirus alone, with no fungus named

explanation: Iridovirus and koi herpesvirus lead to high fish mortality; Saprolegnia causes skin and gill infections.

why.a: Correct. These are the viruses and the fungus the text names.
why.b: Wrong. Neither of these viruses nor Candida appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Rabies and Aspergillus do not appear in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Two viruses are named, and Saprolegnia is named as the fungus.

prompt: The fungus {{1}} causes skin and gill infections in fish.
explanation: Saprolegnia. It is the only fungus named in the course, so it is worth holding on its own.

prompt: Which parasitic worms and protozoa does the text name as weakening fish?

options.text: Ichthyophthirius and Gyrodactylus
Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter
Gallionella and Leptothrix
Vibrio and Pseudomonas

explanation: Ichthyophthirius and Gyrodactylus. Ichthyophthirius is the parasite behind the disease the behaviour unit calls Ich.

why.a: Correct. These two are named under pathogens and parasites.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the beneficial nitrifying bacteria.
why.c: Wrong. Those are iron bacteria.
why.d: Wrong. Those are harmful bacteria, not parasites.

prompt: High {{1}} matter increases the risk of disease outbreaks in a pond.
explanation: Organic matter. It is both its own biological parameter and a driver of the pathogen risk.

prompt: Which three control measures does the text give for pathogens and parasites?

options.text: Regular pond cleaning and water exchange, use of probiotics and biosecurity measures, and proper stocking density to reduce stress
Adding lime, adding potassium permanganate, and installing sand filters
Increasing feeding, raising temperature, and reducing aeration
Manual removal, grass carp, and herbicides

explanation: Cleaning and exchange, probiotics and biosecurity, and correct stocking density. The manual removal and grass carp answer is the macrophyte control list, and the lime and potassium permanganate answer is the iron list.

why.a: Correct. These three are the control measures for pathogens and parasites.
why.b: Wrong. Those are iron treatments.
why.c: Wrong. Every one of those would make a disease outbreak more likely.
why.d: Wrong. Those control macrophytes, the aquatic plants and weeds.

prompt: What is the role of organic matter and decomposers, and what is the risk?

options.text: Natural decomposition recycles nutrients, but excess fish waste, uneaten feed and dead plants lead to oxygen depletion and ammonia buildup
They serve no purpose and must be removed completely
They raise dissolved oxygen and lower ammonia
They only matter in recirculating systems

explanation: Recycling in moderation, oxygen depletion and ammonia buildup in excess. The same pattern as plankton: useful until there is too much of it.

why.a: Correct. Nutrient recycling against oxygen depletion and ammonia buildup.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Decomposition is a natural and useful process.
why.c: Wrong. Excess organic matter consumes oxygen and produces ammonia.
why.d: Wrong, and the word only is misplaced; the risk applies in ponds too.

prompt: Organic matter is controlled by avoiding overfeeding, using {{1}} in recirculating aquaculture systems, and maintaining aeration.
explanation: Biofilters. They house the beneficial bacteria, which is the same reason filter media must not be rinsed in chlorinated tap water.

prompt: What are macrophytes, and how are they controlled?

options.text: Aquatic plants and weeds, controlled by manual removal, biological control with grass carp, or herbicides
Microscopic bacteria, controlled by antibiotics
Suspended solids, controlled by settling tanks
Dissolved minerals, controlled by ion exchange

explanation: Aquatic plants and weeds. They provide shelter and oxygen, but overgrowth competes with fish for oxygen and harbours predators.

why.a: Correct. Macrophytes are aquatic plants and weeds, with those three control measures.
why.b: Wrong. Bacteria are the microbial load, a separate parameter.
why.c: Wrong. Suspended solids are a physical parameter.
why.d: Wrong. Dissolved minerals are chemical.

prompt: Biological control of macrophytes uses grass {{1}}.
explanation: Grass carp. It is the only named biological control agent in the course.

prompt: Which three reasons does the text give for the importance of biological parameters?

options.text: They maintain water quality and ecological balance, reduce disease outbreaks and fish mortality, and enhance natural feed availability and farm productivity
They lower the cost of feed, shorten transport, and raise export prices
They replace the need for chemical and physical monitoring
They increase stocking density without any cost

explanation: Balance, disease reduction, natural feed and productivity. Biological parameters are not a substitute for the other two families, they are the third leg.

why.a: Correct. These three are listed under the importance of biological parameters.
why.b: Wrong. None of these is claimed in the section.
why.c: Wrong. All three families are monitored together.
why.d: Wrong. The text warns that proper stocking density reduces stress.

prompt: Which statement expresses the basic water-quality rule that should guide a prospective fish farmer?

options.text: Eliminate every microorganism, including beneficial bacteria, from the system.
Replace all mechanical filters daily regardless of water conditions.
Do not venture into fish farming without first knowing the quality of the water to be used.
Use only artificial plastic plants in every aquaculture system.

explanation: Test 2, question 25, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. This is the thumb rule the text states word for word at the close of the water quality section.

why.a: Wrong. Every is an absolute, and Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are wanted in the system.
why.b: Wrong. All and daily are absolutes; filter maintenance is monthly.
why.c: Correct. Know the quality of your water before you begin.
why.d: Wrong. Only and every are absolutes, and live plants are recommended as an aeration aid.

prompt: What is the "thumb rule" mentioned regarding entering the fish farming business?

options.text: Always use the most expensive filtration system available
Do not venture into fish farming without knowing the standard of your water
Only use water that appears crystal clear to the naked eye
Feed the fish four times a day to ensure rapid growth

explanation: Test 1, question 21, quoted as printed. The crystal clear answer is the very trap the text warns against: not all waters that are crystal clear are suitable for fish farming.

why.a: Wrong, and an absolute. Cost is never given as the measure of a filtration system.
why.b: Correct. Know the standard of your water before you venture in.
why.c: Wrong. The text says explicitly that clean does not imply safe for rearing fish.
why.d: Wrong. Daily feeding is one to two times, and overfeeding pollutes the water.

prompt: Water that is crystal clear is by that fact suitable for fish farming.
explanation: The text is blunt about this: not all waters that are crystal clear are suitable, and the fact that water is clean does not imply that it is safe for rearing fish. To avoid water testing analysis is to get your fingers burnt.

why.true: Wrong. Clarity is a physical parameter and says nothing about chemistry or biology.
why.false: Correct. Clean is not the same as safe, which is why testing is not optional.

prompt: To avoid water testing analysis is to get your {{1}} burnt.
explanation: Fingers. It is the text's own phrasing, and phrasings this vivid are exactly what a wording question hangs on.

prompt: When evaluating the biological parameter of water, what level of Total Bacterial Count (TBC) is categorized as "High Risk," indicating a high likelihood of bacterial diseases?

options.text: Greater than 1.0 x 10⁵ CFU/mL
Less than 30 NTU
Exactly 5.0 mg/L
Between 1.0 x 10³ and 1.0 x 10⁴ CFU/mL

explanation: Test 1, question 20, quoted as printed. This threshold is not stated in the 88-page course text, so it comes from the lecturer's own material. The units still give it away: CFU per mL counts colonies, which is a biological measure.

why.a: Correct. Greater than 1.0 x 10⁵ CFU/mL is the high risk band, and CFU/mL is the only biological unit offered.
why.b: Wrong. NTU measures turbidity, which is a physical parameter.
why.c: Wrong. mg/L is a chemical concentration; 5.0 mg/L is the floor of the dissolved oxygen range.
why.d: Wrong. This is a lower band, two orders of magnitude below the high risk threshold.

prompt: A high total plate count is commonly associated with {{1}} sanitation.
explanation: Test 2, question 19, quoted as printed. Note the wording: the course text says Total Bacterial Count, and total plate count is the examiner's own phrase for the same measure. Both mean a count of bacterial colonies, and a high one points at poor sanitation.

prompt: How does the glossary define hypoxia?

options.text: A condition in which there is a deficiency of oxygen in a specific environment, such as water, air or living tissues
An excess of oxygen dissolved in water
The over-enrichment of water with nutrients
The presence of iron bacteria in a pond

explanation: A deficiency of oxygen. The glossary widens it beyond water to air and living tissues, which is why iron deposits on gills also produce hypoxia.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry word for word.
why.b: Wrong. That would be the opposite of a deficiency.
why.c: Wrong. Nutrient over-enrichment is eutrophication.
why.d: Wrong. Iron bacteria cause hypoxia indirectly, but they are not its definition.

prompt: Hypoxia is a condition in which there is a deficiency of {{1}} in a specific environment.
explanation: Oxygen. Hypoxia is the word the text uses when dissolved oxygen falls below the 5 to 8 mg/L requirement.

prompt: Eutrophication is defined in the glossary as the process by which a body of water becomes overly enriched with which nutrients?

options.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus
Iron and manganese
Calcium and magnesium
Sodium and chloride

explanation: Nitrogen and phosphorus. The stated sources are runoff containing fertilizers, sewage or animal waste, and the result is excessive growth of algae and other aquatic plants.

why.a: Correct. Nitrogen and phosphorus are the two nutrients named.
why.b: Wrong. Iron is a chemical parameter in its own right, not a eutrophication nutrient here.
why.c: Wrong. Calcium and magnesium relate to hardness.
why.d: Wrong. Sodium and chloride relate to salinity.

prompt: {{1}} is the process by which a body of water becomes overly enriched with nutrients, leading to excessive growth of algae.
explanation: Eutrophication. It is named twice: once as a long-term effect of excess phytoplankton, and once as a risk of excessive plankton growth.

prompt: What are probiotics, according to the glossary?

options.text: Live microorganisms, primarily bacteria and yeast, that provide health benefits when consumed in adequate amounts
Chemicals added to kill all bacteria in a pond
Feed additives that increase fat content
Filters used to remove suspended solids

explanation: Live microorganisms, bacteria and yeast, described as the good or beneficial bacteria. They appear as a control measure for pathogens and parasites.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry word for word.
why.b: Wrong. Probiotics add beneficial organisms rather than killing everything.
why.c: Wrong. No fat-increasing additive is described in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Filters are equipment, not living organisms.

prompt: Biosecurity refers to measures designed to prevent which three things?

options.text: The introduction, spread and impact of infectious diseases, pests and invasive species within a specific area
Theft, vandalism and trespass on the farm
Flooding, erosion and drought
Price fluctuation, currency risk and default

explanation: Introduction, spread and impact. Note that the security of the MAKE principle is about fences and guards; biosecurity is about disease.

why.a: Correct. The glossary names introduction, spread and impact of diseases, pests and invasive species.
why.b: Wrong. That is the MAKE principle of security, which is fencing, CCTV and guards.
why.c: Wrong. Those are environmental risks, not biosecurity.
why.d: Wrong. Those are financial risks handled by risk management.

prompt: Stocking {{1}} is the number of animals or organisms kept within a specific area or volume of space.
explanation: Density, expressed for example as fish per cubic metre. Proper stocking density is listed as a control measure because overcrowding causes stress.

prompt: The self-assessment answer describes what happens when polluted water is left unchanged for two weeks. What does it list?

options.text: Low dissolved oxygen, high acidic content of the water, disease outbreak and eventually death
A rise in dissolved oxygen and faster growth
Clearer water and improved appetite
No measurable change within that period

explanation: Low dissolved oxygen, high acidity, disease outbreak, death. It is the practical case against skipping the weekly partial water change.

why.a: Correct. These four consequences are named in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong. Pollution consumes oxygen rather than adding it.
why.c: Wrong. Stressed fish eat less, and organic load clouds the water.
why.d: Wrong. Two weeks is given precisely because the change is severe.

prompt: Match each chemical parameter to the threshold the text gives for it.
explanation: The five chemical thresholds in one pass. The spare labels are the nitrate ceiling, the high-risk iron level and the tilapia temperature, all of which the examiner uses as distractors.

prompt: Match each named organism to what it does in a fish pond.

pairs.right: Beneficial, breaks down ammonia and nitrate
Fungus, causes skin and gill infections

explanation: Five organisms, five different jobs. Only one of them is on your side.

prompt: Physical parameters are {{1}}, chemical parameters are {{2}}, and biological parameters are {{3}}.

accept: temperature, turbidity, colour, odour and suspended solids
choices: temperature, turbidity, colour, odour and suspended solids
ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals
plankton, microbial load, pathogens, organic matter and macrophytes
filters, pumps, aerators, heaters and nets

accept: ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals
choices: ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals
temperature, turbidity, colour, odour and suspended solids
plankton, microbial load, pathogens, organic matter and macrophytes
stocking density, feeding rate and water exchange rate

accept: plankton, microbial load, pathogens and parasites, organic matter and macrophytes
choices: plankton, microbial load, pathogens and parasites, organic matter and macrophytes
ammonia, salinity, pH, hardness and dissolved minerals
temperature, turbidity, colour, odour and suspended solids
records, budgets, policies and staff training

explanation: The whole classification in one question. Every water quality question in both tests is answered by sorting the measurement into one of these three families first.

prompt: Biological parameters are the {{1}} organisms present in water that can affect fish health, growth and overall farm productivity.
explanation: Living. That single word is the test: if the thing being measured is alive, it is a biological parameter.

prompt: As a thumb rule, do not venture into fish farming without knowing the {{1}} of your water.
explanation: Quality, which the text also phrases as the standard of your water. Both tests asked this rule, once in each paper, so it is the single most examined sentence in the unit.

prompt: Maintaining a balanced biological environment is crucial for disease prevention, water quality management and sustainable fish farming.
explanation: The sentence that opens the biological parameters section. Balance is the word to hold: neither sterile nor overgrown.

why.true: Correct. The text names all three benefits of a balanced biological environment.
why.false: Wrong. The section exists precisely to make this case.
